rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rāzī says proof of the Creator and rejection of partners is followed by proof of prophethood, against the Taʿlīmiyya and Ḥashwiyya accounts of how God is known.
rows.anchor: وذلك يدل على فساد قول التعليمية الذين جعلوا معرفة الله مستفادة من معرفة الرسول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: His first proof considers equal eloquence, a non-miraculous increase, or an extraordinary increase; hostile, eloquent Arabs could answer the challenge if either of the first two applied, so their failure proves the Qur’an miraculous.
rows.anchor: فلما لم يأتوا بها علمنا عجزهم عنها فثبت أن القرآن لا يماثل قولهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rāzī says poets’ quality fell when they committed to truth; he cites Labīd and Ḥassān’s weaker Islamic poetry to stress the Qur’an’s eloquence despite truthfulness.
rows.anchor: وكل شاعر ترك الكذب والتزم الصدق نزل شعره ولم يكن جيدا ألا ترى أن لبيد بن ربيعة وحسان بن ثابت لما أسلما نزل شعرهما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Whereas a fine poem may contain only one or two excellent lines, the Qur’an is eloquent throughout and people cannot match it even as a whole.
rows.anchor: وليس كذلك القرآن لأنه كله فصيح بحيث يعجز الخلق عنه كما عجزوا عن جملته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Poets’ repeated treatment of a subject loses quality, but the Qur’an repeats material without any drop in eloquence.
rows.anchor: ومع ذلك كل واحد منها في نهاية الفصاحة ولم يظهر التفاوت أصلا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an chiefly commands worship, forbids vice, urges virtue and the afterlife—subjects Rāzī says normally reduce eloquence—yet it remains unsurpassed.
rows.anchor: أنه اقتصر على إيجاب العبادات وتحريم القبائح والحث على مكارم الأخلاق وترك الدنيا واختيار الآخرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Unlike poets who excel in particular genres, the Qur’an reaches peak eloquence in promise, threat, admonition, and theology, as its cited passages illustrate.
rows.anchor: أما القرآن فإنه جاء فصيحا في كل الفنون على غاية الفصاحة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an is the source of theology, jurisprudence, legal theory, grammar, language, asceticism, afterlife teaching, and ethics; its eloquence reaches the highest degree in every respect.
rows.anchor: أن القرآن أصل العلوم كلها فعلم الكلام كله في القرآن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: His second proof says either the Qur’an’s eloquence is already inimitable, or imitation was possible but never attempted despite strong motives; either way it is miraculous, and Rāzī prefers this route.
rows.anchor: فثبت أن القرآن معجز على جميع الوجوه وهذا الطريق عندنا أقرب إلى الصواب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rāzī reads نزلنا as gradual revelation: the Qur’an came surah by surah with events, answering the objection that a divine book would have descended all at once.
rows.anchor: على لفظ التنزيل دون الإنزال لأن المراد النزول على سبيل التدريج

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The gradual form does not weaken the challenge: if it were within human capacity, opponents could match it gradually; otherwise its gradual revelation is itself miraculous.
rows.anchor: وجب إتيانهم بمثله أو بما يقرب منه على التدريج

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A reading has the plural على عبادنا, referring to the Messenger and his community.
rows.anchor: وقرىء ( على عبادنا ) يريد رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم وأمته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If the wāw is original, sūra may derive from a city wall: a Qur’anic section is bounded like a walled city or contains branches of knowledge as a wall encloses what is within.
rows.anchor: إن كانت أصلا فإما أن تسمى بسور المدينة وهو حائطها لأنها طائفة من القرآن محدودة كالبلد المسور أو لأنها محتوية على فنون من العلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another proposed derivation from the original wāw connects sūra to rank: the reader advances through levels, and suras themselves are long, medium, or short and exalted in status.
rows.anchor: وإما أن تسمى بالسورة التي هي الرتبة لأن السورة بمنزلة المنازل والمراتب يترقى فيها القارىء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If the wāw replaces hamza, sūra means a piece or remainder, hence a distinct portion of the Qur’an.
rows.anchor: وإن جعلت واوها منقلبة عن همزة فلأنها قطعة وطائفة من القرآن كالسورة التي هي البقية من الشيء والفضلة منه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Dividing the Qur’an into suras serves the same organizational purpose as authors’ chapters and sections, and separates kinds for clarity.
rows.anchor: ما لأجله بوب المصنفون كتبهم أبوابا وفصولا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A reader gains energy and retention by finishing one sura and beginning another, like a traveler encouraged by knowing a mile or league is complete.
rows.anchor: إذا ختم سورة أو بابا من الكتاب ثم أخذ في آخر كان أنشط له وأثبت على التحصيل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A memorizer can take pride and delight in having mastered a self-contained Qur’anic portion; this is one reason a complete sura is preferable in prayer.
rows.anchor: اعتقد أنه أخذ من كتاب الله طائفة مستقلة بنفسها فيجل في نفسه ذلك ويغتبط به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The challenge to produce a sura implies that the Qur’an’s sura arrangement is as God revealed it, contrary to the report that ʿUthmān’s era arranged it; this permits challenge by one sura or the whole Qur’an.
rows.anchor: يدل على القرآن أن وما هو عليه من كونه سورا هو على حد ما أنزله الله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rāzī lists challenges to bring a more-guiding book, the whole Qur’an, ten fabricated suras, or one sura, calling this escalating range the fullest challenge and removal of excuses.
rows.anchor: فإن هذا هو النهاية في التحدي وإزالة العذر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although people might imitate short suras such as al-Kawthar, al-ʿAṣr, or al-Kāfirūn, either their eloquence itself is miraculous or their failure despite motivation is; Rāzī therefore uses his second proof.
rows.anchor: قلنا فلهذا السبب اخترنا الطريق الثاني

rows.speaker: عمر وابن مسعود وابن عباس والحسن وأكثر المحققين
rows.claim: The pronoun in “of its like” refers to what was revealed—the Qur’an—so the challenge is to produce a sura matching its eloquence and composition; Rāzī prefers this reading.
rows.anchor: والأول مروي عن عمر وابن مسعود وابن عباس والحسن وأكثر المحققين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An alternative takes the pronoun to refer to “Our servant”: produce a sura by a human like Muhammad, unlettered and without reading books or learning from scholars.
rows.anchor: أي فأتوا ممن هو على حاله من كونه بشرا أميا لم يقرأ الكتب ولم يأخذ من العلماء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an reading matches other challenge passages, especially the Yunus challenge, which says “bring a sura like it.”
rows.anchor: لا سيما ما ذكره في يونس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The context asks whether the revelation is from God, so the pronoun naturally points back to the revealed text.
rows.anchor: البحث إنما وقع في المنزل لأنه قال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If the pronoun refers to the Qur’an, all people are challenged regardless of whether they act alone or together, and whether literate or unlettered; the Muhammad reading limits the comparison to one unlettered person.
rows.anchor: لأنه لا يكون مثل محمد إلا الشخص الواحد الأمي فأما لو اجتمعوا وكانوا قارئين لم يكونوا مثل محمد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an reading makes the miracle rest on its eloquence; the alternative rests on Muhammad’s illiteracy, which entails a kind of deficiency in him, so Rāzī prefers the first.
rows.anchor: وهذا وإن كان معجزا أيضا إلا أنه لما كان لا يتم إلا بتقرير نوع من النقصان في حق محمد عليه السلام كان الأول أولى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Referring the pronoun to Muhammad could suggest that someone unlike him in illiteracy might produce the Qur’an; referring it to the Qur’an establishes that no literate or unlettered person can.
rows.anchor: لكان ذلك يوهم أن صدور مثله القرآن ممن لم يكن مثل محمد في كونه أميا ممكن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One reading makes the “witnesses” the idols claimed to be gods: calling mute objects to aid the challenge mocks them and attacks both their divinity and the claim that Muhammad invented the Qur’an.
rows.anchor: المراد من ادعوا فيه الإلهية وهي الأوثان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another reading means chiefs, leaders, or supporters who could assist the challengers, arbitrate, and judge whether imitation was possible.
rows.anchor: المراد من الشهداء أكابرهم أو من يوافقهم في إنكار أمر محمد عليه السلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Both readings can fit a shared sense of helpers, so idols and leaders are included; if one must choose, Rāzī prefers human chiefs because “witnesses” literally observe and testify, whereas idols require figurative or implicit wording.
rows.anchor: لفظ الشهداء لا يطلق ظاهرا إلا على من يصح أن يشاهد ويشهد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Dūn first means a lower place or inferior thing; it expands from spatial nearness and lesser rank to crossing from one boundary or allegiance to another.
rows.anchor: ثم اتسع فيه فاستعمل في كل ما يجاوز حدا إلى حد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In 3:28, “besides” means not passing from the believers’ alliance to the unbelievers’ alliance.
rows.anchor: أي لا يتجاوزون ولاية المؤمنين إلى ولاية الكافرين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If “besides God” modifies “your witnesses,” it can mean the idols they worship apart from God, whom they claim will testify for them on Judgment Day; relying on mute objects is derisive.
rows.anchor: ادعوا الذين اتخذتموهم آلهة من دون الله وزعمتم أنهم يشهدون لكم يوم القيامة أنكم على الحق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The same attachment can mean witnesses apart from God’s allies and outside the believers, including eloquence champions whose sound judgment would not let them falsely attest to a match.
rows.anchor: ادعوا شهداءكم من دون الله أي من دون أوليائه ومن غير المؤمنين ليشهدوا لكم أنكم أتيتم بمثله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If “besides God” modifies the act of calling, they must summon human witnesses instead of appealing to God as witness; this leaves no remaining proof for their claim.
rows.anchor: والمعنى ادعوا من دون الله شهداءكم

rows.speaker: القاضي
rows.claim: Al-Qāḍī argues the challenge refutes determinism: denying human agency makes challenge impossible; inability would be ordinary lack of power; God would challenge Himself; custom-breaking would lose its contrast; and divine authorship could not specially verify the Prophet.
rows.anchor: قال القاضي هذا التحدي يبطل القول بالجبر من وجوه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rāzī replies that challenge requires an intentional attempt: an accidental match is outside one’s control, while an intention originating in the agent entails regress and one originating in God restores determinism, undermining al-Qāḍī’s objections.
rows.anchor: أن المطلوب من التحدي إما أن يأتي الخصم بالمتحدى به قصدا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Arab hostility and zeal to discredit Muhammad mean they would have produced a match if able; the added taunt that they will never do so makes their failure proof of the miracle.
rows.anchor: فحيث ما أتوا به ظهر المعجز

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Muhammad was known for judgment and foresight; if he suspected they could answer, he would not have risked such an emphatic challenge and public disgrace.
rows.anchor: فلولا معرفته بالاضطرار من حالهم أنهم عاجزون عن المعارضة لما جوز من نفسه أن يحملهم على المعارضة بأبلغ الطرق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: His certainty that they would never produce a match supports his certainty in his prophethood, since a false claimant would not risk a prediction whose failure exposed him.
rows.anchor: فلما جزم دل على أنه عليه الصلاة والسلام كان قاطعا في أمره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: From Muhammad’s time to Rāzī’s own era, enemies with strong motives to attack Islam never produced a counterexample; this fulfilled prediction is miraculous.
rows.anchor: ثم إنه مع هذا الحرص الشديد لم توجد المعارضة قط

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rāzī concludes these four proofs are contained in the verse, rejecting those who claim the Qur’an offers no evidence or argument.
rows.anchor: فهذه الوجوه الأربعة في الدلالة على المعجز مما تشتمل عليها هذه الآية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The conditional “if” follows the opponents’ own assumption: despite their confidence in eloquence, they had not yet accepted that they were unable to answer.
rows.anchor: أن يساق القول معهم على حسب حسبانهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A second explanation for “if” is mockery: a confident victor may say “if I defeat you” while knowing defeat is certain.
rows.anchor: أن يتهكم بهم كما يقول الموصوف بالقوة الواثق من نفسه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “If you do not” is shorter than repeating “if you do not bring a sura like it.”
rows.anchor: لأن هذا أخصر من أن يقال فإن لم تأتوا بسورة من مثله ولن تأتوا بسورة من مثله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ولن تفعلوا is a parenthetical clause and has no syntactic position.
rows.anchor: لا محل لها لأنها جملة اعتراضية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Lā and lan both negate the future, but lan strengthens the negation.
rows.anchor: لا ولن أختان في نفي المستقبل إلا أن في ( لن ) توكيدا وتشديدا

rows.speaker: الخليل
rows.claim: One reported etymology says lan originated as lā plus an.
rows.anchor: أصله لا أن ، وهو قول الخليل

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ says lan is lā with its alif replaced by nūn.
rows.anchor: لا ، أبدلت ألفها نونا ، وهو قول الفراء

rows.speaker: سيبويه وإحدى الروايتين عن الخليل
rows.claim: Sībawayh and one report from al-Khalīl treat lan as a subjunctive particle that emphasizes future negation.
rows.anchor: حرف نصب لتأكيد نفي المستقبل وهو قول سيبويه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Failure to imitate establishes Muhammad’s truth; persistence in defiance merits punishment, so “guard against the Fire” stands for “abandon stubbornness,” a concise expression that intensifies the threat.
rows.anchor: فاتقاء النار يوجب ترك العناد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Waqūd means what a fire is kindled with; as a verbal noun it is usually pronounced with ḍamma, though fatḥ is also attested.
rows.anchor: هو ما يوقد به النار وأما المصدر فمضوم وقد جاء فيه الفتح

rows.speaker: سيبويه
rows.claim: Sībawayh reports Arabs saying “we kindled the fire with a high flame”; he says the fuel noun is the more common form and can mean firewood.
rows.anchor: قال سيبويه : وسمعنا من العرب من يقول

rows.speaker: عيسى بن عمر
rows.claim: ʿĪsā ibn ʿUmar reads waqūd with ḍamma, treating it as a verbal noun, like fakhr or zayn.
rows.anchor: وقرأ عيسى بن عمر بالضم تسمية بالمصدر كما يقال فلان فخر قومه وزين بلده

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: People could know that the afterlife fire is fueled by people and stones from earlier teaching by People of the Book, the Prophet, or the earlier verse in al-Taḥrīm.
rows.anchor: لا يمنع أن يتقدم لهم بذلك سماع من أهل الكتاب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Taḥrīm 66:6 calls it an indefinite fire because it was revealed in Mecca; al-Baqara uses the definite fire in Medina, referring to what they had already learned.
rows.anchor: فعرفوا منها نارا موصوفة بهذه الصفة ثم نزلت هذه بالمدينة مستندة إلى ما عرفوه أولا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This fire is distinguished because it burns directly from the people and stones it consumes, unlike ordinary fires first kindled with fuel; its extreme heat also ignites stone.
rows.anchor: أن سائر النيران إذا أريد إحراق الناس بها أو إجماء الحجارة أوقدت أولا بوقود
